pass_a_gloss: Tome 2. [Lemma, Isaiah 13:1:] Vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Babylon. The vision against Babylon, and indeed also those after it in order, against the Idumaeans and Moabites, and moreover also the Egyptians, and besides that the others, have been made for comfort to Israel; they have a somewhat more historical rendering of the things signified, except that it is allowed to the more sensible, as from a thick image here too, to recast elegantly into spiritual contemplation, most clear, the things that befell the ancients; which the discourse, going forward, will make into a narration for those who will come upon it, interpreting each of the things written as far as possible. And I think it needful now too to run back to the beginning of the affair and to narrate beforehand the causes of the vision. For Israel, having been called through the all-wise Moses into knowledge and worship of the God who truly is, and having a law that directs toward anything whatever of things admired, neglected the commandment given to him, and turned to teachings, commandments of men; rather, letting himself into things still worse, he slipped into the pits of idol worship. So the God of all accused, through every prophet, those who chose to do such things, and made a great outcry against him for having been impious. He said, then: This people draws near to me, with their lips they honour me, but their heart is far away from me. In vain they revere me, teaching teachings, commandments of men. And again: Why has the beloved done abomination in my house? And abomination he names the idol. So, them having turned aside terribly into outlandish corruptions, and carrying their neck away from the slavery under God, and raising up against him, haughty as it were, their own mind, he handed them over at times, sometimes to those who occupy the neighbouring country, Idumaeans I mean, and indeed Moabites too, Egyptians and those from the Philistines; and sometimes, bringing on them a heavier blow, he let loose upon them those most cruel of all on earth, I mean the Babylonians, who, ravaging without toil the whole land of the Jews, carried away captive to their own land a multitude beyond number. But that these things will happen to them as they provoke the God of all, the blessed prophets foretold at times. But they, although the things already announced had come to an end for them, none the less [the section breaks off].

lemmas.gloss: those who will come upon it, readers

pass_b_english: Tomos 2. “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Babylon” (Isaiah 13:1).

The vision against Babylon, and the visions that follow it in order, against the Edomites and the Moabites, and against the Egyptians too, and besides these against the other nations, were composed to comfort Israel. They set out what they mean in a rather historical way. Yet the more discerning may, here as well, skilfully recast the things that befell the ancients, as from a coarse image, into a spiritual contemplation that is very clear. As the discourse goes on, it will set this out for those who read it, interpreting each thing written as far as it can.

But I think it necessary here too to go back to the beginning of the matter and first to relate the causes of the vision. Israel had been called through the all-wise Moses to the knowledge and worship of Him who is truly God, and had the Law to guide him straight toward everything worthy of admiration. Yet he neglected the commandment given to him and turned to teachings that are the commandments of men (Isaiah 29:13); or rather, giving himself over to things still worse, he slipped into the pits of idolatry.

So the God of all, through every prophet, accused those who chose to do such things, and raised a loud outcry against Israel for his impiety. He said, for example: “This people draws near to Me; with their lips they honour Me, but their heart is far from Me. In vain they worship Me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8-9). And again: “Why has the beloved done an abomination in My house?” (Jeremiah 11:15). By “abomination” he means the idol.

So when they had turned terribly aside into outlandish corruptions, pulling their neck out from service under God and raising up against Him a mind of their own, as if in pride, He handed them over from time to time. Sometimes He gave them to those who held the neighbouring land, I mean the Edomites, and the Moabites as well, the Egyptians and the Philistines. At other times He brought a heavier blow on them and let loose against them the cruellest of all who are on earth, I mean the Babylonians, who laid waste the whole land of the Jews without effort and carried off a multitude past counting as captives to their own land.

The blessed prophets foretold time after time that these things would happen to them as they provoked the God of all. Yet they, even though what had been foretold had already come to pass upon them, none the less…

choices.why: The verb is used of re-striking a coin; the more discerning re-shape the historical sense into a spiritual one.
ἐφεῖται grants permission; it is not a statement that only they can do it.
ἐντυγχάνω here is reading a book, the usual sense with a written discourse.
The Law is the subject that directs Israel; the participle keeps its active sense.
Cyril himself glosses the word as the idol in the next sentence, so the Scripture word is kept.
